entities.summary:
Sophia of Bavaria (c. 1105 – July 17, 1145) was a pivotal German noblewoman whose strategic marriages profoundly influenced the dynastic landscape of the Holy Roman Empire in the early 12th century. A member of the powerful Welf dynasty, her unions with Berthold III, Duke of Zähringen, and Leopold I, Margrave of Styria, cemented crucial alliances and facilitated the transfer of significant territorial claims. Her life exemplifies the critical role aristocratic women played in medieval politics, often serving as living instruments of peace treaties, territorial consolidation, and dynastic succession, thereby shaping the emerging feudal structures of southern Germany and Austria.

Born around 1105, Sophia was the daughter of Henry IX, Duke of Bavaria, and Wulfhild of Saxony, making her a grandniece of Emperor Henry IV. Her first marriage, before 1122, to Berthold III, Duke of Zähringen, linked the Welfs with the influential Zähringen house, which controlled vast territories in Swabia and Burgundy. This alliance was particularly significant during the Investiture Controversy's aftermath, when regional power balances were in flux. Following Berthold III's death in 1122 without issue, Sophia remarried in 1128 to Leopold I, Margrave of Styria, from the House of Traungau. This second union produced at least four children, most notably Ottokar III, who would succeed his father as Margrave of Styria, and Conrad, who became Archbishop of Salzburg.
